analytic.title: Schedulability Driven Security Optimization in Real-time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper presents EDF schedulability driven security optimization in real-time systems. An increasing number of real-time applications like aircraft control and medical electronics systems require high quality of security to assure confidentiality and integrity of information. However, security requirements were not adequately considered in most existing real-time systems. We propose a group based security service model for real-time systems where the services are partitioned into groups. Services in the same security group provide the same type of security service but of different quality due to the different mechanism used. Service from different groups can be combined to achieve better security. The overhead model of the security services is also described. We consider EDF scheduling policy and develop a security aware EDF schedulability test. Two approaches: Integer Linear Programming technique and an efficient heuristic search technique are proposed to select the best combination of security services for real-time systems while guaranteeing their schedulability.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Communications are essential in modern real-time applications. For example, a radar tracking and processing system needs to read the images from the tracking subsystem periodically and send the tracking commands and directions to the tracking subsystem. A real-time quote and trading system needs to respond to service requests from clients. An increasing number of real-time applications like aircraft control, medical electronics or real-time stock systems require high quality of security to guarantee the messages between the subsystems not being read or altered by malicious users, to control that only the persons or subsystems with the access right be able to access the system, and to guarantee the user really be whom he or she claims to be.

To address these security requirements, security services like message encryption and decryption, secure connection establishment, digital signature verification, authorization access control and credentials validation etc can be used. A system can use one single security service or several services together. Obviously, the more services used, the more secure the system will be. The quality of security of the system also differs when choosing different security mechanism from a particular security group. For example, RC4, RC5 or DES are different mechanisms used for encryption and their quality of security are different [18]. Applying security services to a system incurs overhead to the system including more CPU and memory usage. We only consider CPU overhead of the security services in this paper. We propose a group based security model where the services are partitioned into groups. Services in the same security group provide the same type of security service but of different quality due to the different mechanism used. Services from different groups can be combined to achieve better security. Each security service has a quality value and parameter to compute its overhead.

Real-time systems require not only logical correctness, but also timing correctness. A vehicle with the ability to brake is not enough, it must also be able to brake in time. The timing constraints of a real-time system are often specified as deadlines. It is desirable (required in many cases) for the system to respond within the specified deadline. If such a condition is violated, then it might cause economic losses or even physical damage. Therefore, Predictability is a major concern in a real-time system [5,11,14]. Static schedulability analysis can be used to predict whether the timing constraints of a real-time system can be met [2,7]. We consider Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling policy. We develop a security aware EDF schedulability test which takes into account the security service overhead.

The problem of finding the best combination of services is a combinatorial optimization problem [8]. A naive method would be to exhaustively check all the possible service combinations. This method is obviously too expensive. Two approaches are proposed to select the best combination of security services for real-time systems while guaranteeing their schedulability. One is Integer Linear Programming technique and the other is a search technique. The search technique is efficient since heuristics are developed to pruning the branches and back jumping are used to reduce the search space.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents related works. Section 3 describes system model including task model and security model. Section 4 presents the security aware schedulability test. Section 5 describes the security optimization problem and the two approaches to solve the problem. Section 6 describes the conclusions and future works.

div.head: Related Works
div.p: Works have been done to address security issue [12,13] or more general QoS issues [1] in real-time systems. Xie et al. [17] have presented challenges and open issues in security-aware real-time scheduling for distributed systems. The focus of that work is to design dynamic scheduling algorithm to schedule real-time tasks to achieve high security of the system while maintaining low miss rate of the tasks. However, the problem of predictability in a real-time system with security requirement were not addressed in the these works. Our work addresses static schedulability driven security optimization.

The schedulability analysis needs an overhead model. Irvine and Levin [6] proposed a security taxonomy and overhead framework. While developing a real-time task allocation scheme, which can meet both timing and security constraints of parallel applications on clusters, Xie et al. [16,18] proposed a level based security model. They have studied and performed experiments for three types security services: confidentiality, authentication techniques and data integrity. Similar to the level based security model, our group based security model assumes that a system can have different services of different quality. The difference is that we partition the services into groups and address the effect of combining different types of services to enhance the security of a real-time system.

div.head: Task Model
div.p: We consider a task set T with N independent, preemptable periodic tasks to be scheduled on a single processor. A periodic task t k is identified by the four tuple < e k , p k , D k , M k > where:
• e k is the (worst case) execution time of the task;
• p k is the period of the task;
• D k is the relative deadline of the task;
• M k is the number of data items in the message that need security service.

Note that < e k , p k , D k > is a common model for representing a real-time task [7]. The worst execution time can be derived using high level program analysis [9,10] and low level program analysis that considers platform features [4]. What we add here is the communication factor of a task that need security service.

div.head: Security Model
div.p: Next, we present a general model to specify the security services of the systems.

div.head: Security Services
div.p: A system may provide many security services. we partition the security services into groups where the services in the same group provide the same type of service but of different quality due to the different mechanism used. For example, we can have a group of services for encrypting messages specifically and another group of services for access control etc. We can use RC4, RC5 or DES for message encryption. Their quality are different. Security services from different groups can be combined to achieve better service.

Assume there are Ng groups of security services. Each group contains different security services that provide the same type of security, but has different quality. We use NS i to indicate the number of services in group G i and use S ij to indicate the j th service in the i th group. Each security service has a quality. We assume that the highest quality of service in each group is 1 and the other services have quality value between 0 and 1. We can think of the quality value of each service is a value compared to the group's best security service. We order the services in an increased order of their quality. Each service incurs CPU and memory overhead to the systems. In this paper, we mainly focus on the CPU overhead and consider two main factors that introduce overhead to the system. The first one is the overhead to establish (initialize) the service and the second one is the unit overhead to apply the security mechanism to the messages. We use a three tuple to represent a security service
div.formula: S ij : < Q ij , I ij , U ij > where:
div.p: • Q ij indicates the quality for service S ij ;
• I ij indicates the overhead for initialization of the service S ij ;
• U ij indicates the unit overhead for applying the service S ij to one data item;

div.head: Security Overhead
div.p: We assume the tasks in the whole system select the same set of security services. The CPU overhead of applying service S ij to a real-time system with a task set T can be computed as follows.
div.formula: O ij = N k=1 (I ij + U ij * M k ).
div.p: where M k is the message (the number of data items) in task t k that the security service performs on. Achieving higher quality requires higher overhead to the system. That is, for any two security services S ij and S ij within the same group, if
div.formula: Q ij < Q ij , then we have O ij < O ij .
div.p: We order the services of each group in a decreasing order according to the quality. We have: for any j and j service in a group i, if j < j , then we have
div.formula: • Q ij > Q ij , • O ij > O ij for any task set.

div.head: Combining Security Services
div.p: The services from different groups can be combined together. The question is: how do we compute the quality of the combined service. The combined value depends on the weight of each group. We assign weights to each group (type of service) with the sum of the weights for all the groups as 1. By simply compute the weighted sum of quality values of the selected services, we can derive the quality value for the combined services. Let us use W i to denote the weight of the i th group.

div.head: Security Requirement
div.p: There are two types of security requirements.

• First of all, we can specify the minimal security value for each type (or group) of service. Let M inGQ i denote the minimal security required for the i th service group. It means that the quality value of the selected service in group i must not be less than M inGQ i . The minimal group securities can be represented as a vector
div.formula: < M inGQ 1 . . . M inGQ i . . . M inGQ Ng > .
div.p: • Second, we can specify the minimal combined security value. Remember that the combined security value is the weighted sum of the quality value of the individual services. We use M inQ to denote this required minimal combined security value.

div.head: Security Aware EDF Schedulability Test
div.p: An Earliest Deadline First (EDF) [15] based real-time system schedules tasks according to their deadline. EDF scheduling policy is the optimal scheduling policy for independent preemptable task scheduling on single processor meaning that if a set of tasks are scheduleable by any scheduler, then they are scheculable by an EDF scheduler. A good property of EDF scheduling is that we can decide the schedulability of a set of tasks statically.

Next, we present the EDF schedulability analysis. Let's define the density of a task t k as e k min(D k ,p k ) where e k , D k and p k are the execution time, deadline and the period for task t k . To verify whether a set of tasks are schedulable under EDF scheduling policy, we can use a very simple and robust schedulability test by checking:
div.formula: N k=1 e k min(D k , p k ) ≤ 1
div.p: . This test follows directly from the following theorem [7].
Theorem A system of independent, preemptable tasks can be feasibly scheduled on one processor if the density of the system is equal to or less than 1.
We use δE = N k=1 e k min(D k ,p k ) to represent the original density of the system. Now we show that how to compute the new density of the system when considering security service overhead.
Remember that the CPU overhead of applying service S ij to a real-time system with a task set T can be computed as follows.
div.formula: O ij = N k=1 (I ij + U ij * M k ).
div.p: We define δ ij as the extra density of applying service S ij to the system. we have
div.formula: δ ij = I ij * N k=1 1 min(D k , p k ) + U ij * N k=1 M k min(D k , p k ) .
div.p: Let
div.formula: C 1 = N k=1 1 min(D k , p k ) ,
div.p: and
div.formula: C 2 = N k=1 M k min(D k , p k ) .
div.p: δ ij can be computed as
div.formula: δ ij = C 1 * I ij + C 2 * U ij .
div.p: We define δS as the total extra density of applying all the services in this combination.
The security aware schedulability test then becomes:
div.formula: δE + δS ≤ 1.

div.head: Security Optimization for EDF based Realtime Systems
div.p: To achieve high quality of a real-time system, we can combine services from two or more groups. The services in the same group provide the same type of service, therefore, only one service can be selected from one group. It is possible that we do not need all types of services for a system. To allow no service be selected from a group, one just needs to add an idle service to this group. The idle service's Q, I and U values are set to 0. Not selecting any service from a group means selecting an idle service from the group.
A combination of services is represented as a vector

is the group number and s i is the service selected from group i. The quality value and overhead parameters for s i are < Q i , I i , U i >. Our goal is to maximize the weighted sum of quality values Q = Ng i=1 W i * Q i subject to the following constraints:
1. Only one service is selected from each group.
2. Minimal group-security quality constraint: the security value of the selected service in each group has to be bigger than or equal to the minimal required security value for that group. That is
div.formula: Q i ≥ M inGQ i , for any i (1 ≤ i ≤ Ng).
div.p: 3. Minimal combined-security quality constraint: the combined security has to be not less than the minimal required combined security. That is,
div.formula: Q ≥ M inQ, where Q = Ng i=1 W i * Q i .
div.p: 4. Schedulability constraint: the overhead will not make the system utilization larger than 1. Remember that δE = N k=1 e k min(D k ,p k ) is the original density of the system. And δ ij , the extra density of applying service S ij to the the system is:
div.formula: δ ij = I ij * N k=1 1 min(D k , p k ) +U ij * N k=1 M k min(D k , p k ) .
div.p: δS, the total extra density of applying all the services in this combination can be computed as:
div.formula: δS = C 1 * Ng i=1 I i + C 2 * Ng i=1 U i .
div.p: where
div.formula: C 1 = N k=1 1 min(D k , p k ) , C 2 = N k=1 M k min(D k , p k ) .
div.p: The schedulability test requires that:
div.formula: δE + δS ≤ 1.
div.p: The problem of finding the best combination is a combinatorial optimization problem [8]. A naive method would be to exhaustively check all the possible service combinations. This method is obviously too expensive. Next, we provide two methods to solve the problem.

div.head: Using the Integer Linear Programming Technique
div.p: The first method to solve the problem is the Integer Linear Programming (ILP) technique. What needs to be done is to formulate the problem as an ILP problem.
First, we need to define the variables of the system under consideration. Then we shall express the goal and the constraints over the defined variables.

For each service of a group, we define a variable A ij where i represents the group number (1 ≤ i ≤ Ng) and j represents the service number ((1 ≤ i ≤ NS i ). A ij being either 1 or 0 indicates that the j th service of the i th group is selected or not selected to apply to the system.
Our aim is to find an assignment for each A ij to maximize the combined security of the system subject to the minimal security requirement constraint and the Schedulability constraint.
The goal function can be expressed as
div.formula: max Q = Ng i=1 W i * Q i = Ng i=1 W i * ( NSi j=1 A ij * Q ij ).
div.p: There are four types of constraints:
1. First, only one service is selected from each group. Therefore, for each group i (1 ≤ i ≤ Ng), we have one constraint:
div.formula: NSi j=1 A ij = 1.
div.p: 2. Minimal group-security quality constraint: the quality of the selected service from any group has to be not less than the minimal required quality value for that group. Therefore, for each group i where (1 ≤ i ≤ Ng), we have one constraint:
div.formula: Q i = NSi j=1 A ij * Q ij ≥ M inGQ i .
div.p: 3. Minimal combined-security quality constraint: the combined quality of the selected service can not be less than the minimal required value. That is:
div.formula: Q = Ng i=1 W i * ( NSi j=1 A ij * Q ij ) ≥ M inQ.
div.p: 4. Schedulability constraint: the system should still be able to pass the EDF schedulability test with the overhead incurred with the selected services.
div.formula: δE + Ng i=1 NS i j=1 A ij * δ ij ≤ 1,
div.p: where
div.formula: δ ij = C 1 * I ij + C 2 * U ij . C 1 = N k=1 1 min(D k , p k ) . C 2 = N k=1 M k min(D k , p k ) .
div.p: The ILP program can be solved using available tools like Linbox.

div.head: Using a Search Technique
div.p: The second method is a search-based method. First we formulate the problem as a search problem in a graph and then we will use a search technique to solve the problem. The algorithm is efficient since some heuristics are applied to reduce the search space.

We first construct a graph which contains Ng layers. Each layer contains several nodes. A node is a pair < i, j > where i indicates the group number and j indicates the service number. Node < i, j > resides at the j th position of the i th layer.

A path P = s 1 , s 2 . . . s l , (l ≤ Ng) in the graph is a sequence of nodes chosen from each layer in order, where l is the length of the path. A path can be complete or incomplete. A complete path contains one node from each layer while an incomplete path contains fewer nodes than Ng.
A path P = s 1 , s 2 . . . s l passes a node < i, j > iff s i = j ∧ i ≤ l. The quality value of a path P = s 1 , . . . , s l , denoted by Q(P ), is defined as:
div.formula: Q(P ) = l i=1 (W i * Q i ).
div.p: where Q i is the quality value of the s th i service in the i th group. We define δS(P ) as the extra density incurred by the services selected in the path. Both Q(P ) and δS(P ) can be computed incrementally meaning the if we add a new node into a path P , we can add the new quality value and the δS of the node to derive the new Q(P ) and δS(P ). A path P is infeasible if and only if P violates one of the four types of constraints. Otherwise, P is said to be feasible.

A complete path P = s 1 , s 2 , . . . , s N g corresponds to a service combination S =< s 1 , s 2 , . . . , s N g > in the original problem. The aim for the search problem is to find a feasible complete path with maximal combined quality value.

To solve the problem, we use depth-first search [3] with backtracking. We have developed three kinds of heuristics to guide the search procedure and cut branches. The three types of pruning factors are the following.

1. The first type of pruning eliminate the nodes in each layer whose quality value is smaller than the minimal required group-security. We call this group quality pruning. This type of pruning greatly reduce the search space. Fig. 2 shows the quality value of each service of the four groups and the required minimal group security value in the MinGQ vector. Obviously, service S 13 , S 14 , S 23 and S 44 can be eliminated before the search starts. 2. Some branches can be pruned because the incomplete path tested already fails the schedulability test. The search is realized by expanding nodes and backtracking. It wastes time in continuing expansion when a path is found to be infeasible. This is because any path with an infeasible path as prefix is still an infeasible path. Therefore, the paths expanded from an infeasible path can be pruned. We call this Schedulability pruning.

Let's consider an example with 4 groups (Fig. 3) where group 1 has 3 services and the other two groups have 3 services. Suppose the current path is P =< 1, 1 > , < 2, 2 >, < 3, 1 > (see Fig. 3 (b)) and δS(P ) violates the schedulability test. Therefore, path P is not a feasible path. We should not extend this path any further. That is, the paths shown in Fig. 3 (d) (e) and (f ), will be pruned. The immediately subsequent path considered during search is shown in Fig. 3 (c). ity bound: some branches can be pruned since the path's combined quality can not exceed that of the feasible path found before. We called such pruning Quality Bound Pruning.
It is easy to prove (remember that the services of each group are ordered by decreasing quality) that path P = s 1 , . . . , s Ng has a smaller combined quality value than
div.formula: P = s 1 , . . . , s Ng if ∀i((1 ≤ i ≤ Ng) → (Q i ≤ Q i )).
div.p: P has the following property w.r.t. P : at any level, the node selected for P is on the right-hand side of that selected for P . Next, we show look-ahead and backjumping mechanisms to prune subsequent paths with such a property.
With the back jumping, the search may jump a few levels up. The level to jump to is derived based on the following two observations.
• An increment at the final level of a path will not lead to a larger combined quality than the original path. Therefore, the level is at most N -1.

• If the node of a path P at every level from L to Ng is in the leftmost position, then increasing P at any level between L-1 and N will not produce a larger combined quality value than the original path P . Therefore, the backtracking level can be set to L -2.

The levels to jump to are 3, 1, 0, respectively, for the paths shown in Fig. 4 Let P be the complete path found that has the maximal combined quality Q. If Q < M inQ, then it is not possible to find a feasible combination of services that satisfy both the security requirement and schedulability requirement.

div.head: A Special Case: Service Selection from a Single Group
div.p: When there is only one group of security services in the system, the index for the group number is always 1. Remember that our goal is to select the best security service and guarantee the schedulability of the system. If the i th service is the optimal service, it must satisfy the security aware EDF schedulability test which includes the service overhead.

We first compute the maximal allowed density overhead as 1 -δE. Then we compute the density overhead for all the services in the group and store them in a vector. We use binary search on the vector to find the service that has the maximal density overhead which does not exceed 1 -δE. We then check if the quality value constraints are met for the service found. If yes, then we find the optimal security service. Otherwise, the system is not feasible.

div.head: Conclusions and Future Works
div.p: This paper presents EDF schedulability driven security optimization in real-time systems. We have proposed a group based security model where the services are partitioned into groups. Services in the same security group provide the same type of security service but of different quality due to the different mechanism used. Service from different groups can be combined to achieve better security. Applying security services to a system incurs overhead to the system. The overhead model of a security service has also been described. We consider EDF scheduling policy and have developed a security aware EDF schedulability test which takes the density of security service into account. Two approaches are proposed to select the best combination of security services for real-time systems while guaranteeing their schedulability. One is Integer Linear Programming technique and the other is a heuristic search technique. The search technique is efficient since pruning and back jumping are used to reduce the search space.

Currently, we assume all the tasks in the whole system select the same set of security service. In the future, we will allow each task be assigned its own set of security services. We also plan to extend the work to consider fixed priority scheduling.
